summary:
Charter's newsletter combines an AI and Work Radar roundup with an excerpt from its new research playbook, "Redesigning work for the AI era," developed with Council Advisors and featuring cases from EY and Zapier.

Radar items: Gallup finds regular workplace AI use concentrated among those already in quality jobs, with uneven benefits. The Wall Street Journal reports businesses struggle to budget for AI as costs grow unpredictable and cheaper models gain share, with OpenAI's lower-priced GPT-5.6 models helping it close in on Anthropic for business customers; cheaper models can burn more tokens and cost more than pricier ones. A special Edelman Trust Barometer workplace report finds workers rate AI above their managers for creative thinking, hard problem solving, and learning technical skills, with managers winning only on making employees feel valued. A study from the University of Zurich, University of Limerick, and SKEMA Business School found participants in a virtual-reality office paid female-presenting AI agents less than male-presenting ones for identical work.

The main feature is an interview with Joseph Fuller, Harvard Business School professor and Monitor Group co-founder, on entry-level work. Fuller says job postings for entry-level roles have been significantly curtailed in AI-exposed sectors such as financial services and software, and job description contents are changing at a historically high rate. His advice: you cannot have a 10-year-old without a one-year-old, so do not eliminate the pipeline that builds contextual intelligence through experiential learning. If a role is uneconomical, rewrite the job description to add tasks previously reserved for more senior staff, and plan for needs seven or eight years out. At one tech company, junior technical hires were placed on product management teams and sales calls to broaden them beyond silos. On hiring, he recommends work-based learning opportunities to reduce involuntary attrition costs, and structured interviews where different interviewers cover different material in different ways.
